title: Cognate or Con?
intro: Some English words that look Spanish really do mean the same thing. Many don't. Here you practise telling the true friends from the impostors.

A2.q: What does 'notice' mean as a verb?
options: to see or become aware of something
A2.why: As a verb, “notice” means see or become aware of something; Spanish “noticia” is “news”.
A “rope” is a thick cord, like a cowboy's lasso. Spanish “ropa” is “clothes”.
A “diary” is a personal journal. A daily newspaper, Spanish “diario”, is a “newspaper”.
“Parents” are only your mother and father. Spanish “parientes”, all your relatives, are “relatives”.
A “pie” is a dish baked in pastry, sweet or savoury. Spanish “pie” is your “foot”.
“Red” is simply a colour. Spanish “red”, a network or net, is “network” or “net”.
A true friend: “important” means the same as Spanish “importante”.
“Attend” means go to: attend a meeting, attend Mass. “Atender el teléfono” is “answer the phone”.

options: special clothes for a play or party
a habit or custom, like Spanish costumbre
A2.why: A “costume” is fancy dress for a play or Carnival. A habit, Spanish “costumbre”, is a “custom”.
“Soap” is for washing. Spanish “sopa” is “soup”: only one of these goes in the bowl.

options: a place where people stay in tents
A2.why: A “camp” is a place with tents, like a cattle drive's night camp. Spanish “campo” is “countryside” or “field”.

options: a rubber bag filled with air
A2.why: A “balloon” floats at a party. A ball you kick, Spanish “balón”, is a “ball”.

B1.why: “Advertise” means promote publicly. Spanish “advertir”, to warn, is “warn”.

B1.q: What does 'college' mean in British English?
options: a place to study after 16, or part of a university
a primary or secondary school, like Spanish colegio
B1.why: A British “college” is for study after 16 or part of a university; Spanish “colegio” is simply a “school”.

options: a million million, like Spanish billón
B1.why: An English “billion” is a thousand million. Spanish “billón” is a million million, a “trillion”.
A “vase” holds flowers. A drinking glass, Spanish “vaso”, is a “glass”.

options: someone who leads an orchestra, or a train official
B1.why: A “conductor” leads an orchestra or checks tickets. The person driving a car is the “driver”.
A “recipient” is a person who receives something. Spanish “recipiente” is a “container”.

options: a calm conversation about a topic
B1.why: An English “discussion” is calm. A heated “discusión” in Spanish is an “argument”.

B1.q: What does 'notice' mean as a noun?
B1.why: As a noun, a “notice” is a written sign or announcement. Spanish “noticia” is “news”.
“Remove” means take away: remove a stain. To stir the paella, Spanish “remover”, is “stir”.

options: a list of things to discuss at a meeting
a diary for appointments, like Spanish agenda
B1.why: An English “agenda” is a meeting's list of topics. Your appointments book is a “diary”.

B1.q: What does 'record' mean in English, as a verb?
B1.why: To “record” is to store sound or write something down. Spanish “recordar” is “remember”.

options: a person from another country, like Spanish extranjero
B1.why: A “stranger” is someone you don't know. A person from another country is a “foreigner”.

B2.why: “Disgrace” means shame. Spanish “desgracia”, a misfortune, is “misfortune” or “tragedy”.

B2.q: What does 'petrol' mean in British English?
B2.why: In Britain cars run on “petrol”. Crude oil, Spanish “petróleo”, is “oil” or “petroleum”.

options: naive or innocent, like Spanish cándido
B2.why: “Candid” means frank and honest. Spanish “cándido”, naive, is “naive” in English.

options: to talk down to someone, as if you are superior
to be kind and willing to help
B2.why: To “condescend” is to talk down to people; Spanish “condescendiente” (kind, willing to please) is “accommodating” or “obliging”.

options: brave or gallant, like Spanish bizarro
B2.why: A con: “bizarre” means very strange, while traditional Spanish “bizarro” means brave or gallant.
“Exquisite” means extremely fine and delicate, but everyday tasty food, Spanish “exquisito”, is more naturally “delicious”.

options: a chemical added to food to keep it fresh
B2.why: A “preservative” keeps food fresh. Careful: Spanish “preservativo” is a “condom”.

options: friendliness or likeability, like Spanish simpatía
B2.why: “Sympathy” means feeling sorry for someone. Spanish “simpatía” is “friendliness” or “charm”.

options: to include as a necessary part
B2.why: The job involves travelling. To wrap a present, Spanish “envolver”, is “wrap”.

options: a street protest, like Spanish manifestación
B2.why: A fever can be a manifestation of infection. A street protest is a “demonstration”.

options: the part of a shirt around the neck
B2.why: A “collar” is on a shirt or a dog. Spanish “collar”, jewellery, is a “necklace”.
An “injury” is physical harm: a broken leg. Spanish “injuria”, an insult, is “insult” or “slander”.

C1.why: “Ostentatious” means showy, designed to impress: an ostentatious gold watch.
“Notorious” means famous for something bad, like a notorious outlaw; Spanish “notorio” (well-known, obvious) is “well-known” or “evident”.
“Ingenious” means clever and inventive. Spanish “ingenuo”, naive, is “naive” or “ingenuous”.

C1.q: What does 'diversion' mean in British English?
options: an alternative route when a road is closed, or a distraction
C1.why: In Britain a “diversion” is a detour or a distraction; everyday fun, Spanish “diversión”, is just “fun”.

options: happening at the end of a process
possible or maybe, like Spanish eventual
C1.why: “Eventual” means final, in the end. Spanish “eventual”, possible or temporary, is “possible” or “temporary”.

options: to expect something and prepare for it
to do something earlier than planned, like Spanish anticipar
C1.why: “Anticipate” means expect and prepare. To bring something forward, Spanish “anticipar”, is “bring forward”.

options: to believe something is true without proof
to accept a painful fact, like Spanish 'asumirlo'
C1.why: “Assume” means suppose without proof (or take on, as in assume control), but accepting a painful fact, Spanish “asumirlo”, is “accept” or “come to terms with”.

C1.q: What does 'contest' mean in English, as a verb?
C1.why: To “contest” a decision is to challenge it. Spanish “contestar”, to answer, is “answer” or “reply”.

options: to deliberately pay no attention to
not to know something, like Spanish ignorar
C1.why: To “ignore” is to choose not to notice. Not knowing something is “not know” or “be unaware of”.

options: a product that can be bought and sold
C1.why: Oranges and oil are commodities. Spanish “comodidad” is “comfort” or “convenience”.

options: having a bad habit, like Spanish vicioso
C1.why: A “vicious” attack is cruel and violent, a much stronger word than Spanish “vicioso”.

options: a residential area on the edge of a city
a poor neighbourhood, like Spanish suburbio
C1.why: English suburbs are usually quiet and comfortable. A slum, Spanish “suburbio”, is not a suburb.
